en: Stage Director Chamberlain:
Bādarāyaṇa, the servant of Duryodhana.
Duryodhana: the eldest son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra Vāsudeva: Kṛṣṇa, the incarnation of Viṣṇu
Sudarśana: the discus of Vāsudeva Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
king of Hastināpura
The Messenger’s Speech. At the conclusion of the benediction, the Stage Manager enters. The Stage Manager:
May that foot of Upendra, which brings joy to all the worlds, protect you—that foot by which, with its copper-hued nails, the serpent Namuci was torn asunder in the sky. 1.
Thus I inform the noble sirs.
Ah! While I am thus occupied in making this request, what indeed is this sound that is heard? Listen!
I see. (Offstage) O attendants in charge of the gate! His Majesty King Duryodhana issues this command:
Sūtradhāra:
Let it be so; it is understood.
Now that the hostility between the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the Pāṇḍavas has arisen.
The servant constructs the mantra-hall by the command of Duryodhana.
[He] has departed.
[This is] the stage direction. Then enters the chamberlain.
Chamberlain: Ho there, officers in charge of the gate! His Majesty King Duryodhana issues this command: today, together with all the kings—
"I wish to consult;
therefore, let all the kings be summoned.
(Walking about and looking around) Ah, here he is!
The great king Duryodhana is approaching from this very direction—
he who is this dark-complexioned youth with a white silk upper garment, holding an excellent parasol and chowries, and adorned with fragrant unguents.
The glorious one, his limbs adorned by the radiance of his jeweled ornaments, was like the moon at the full moon festival situated in the midst of the stars.
Then enters Duryodhana as described.
Duryodhana: My heart has become filled with joy, as if its anger had been stirred up.
Reflecting suddenly upon this festival of battle,
I desire to see the tusks of the choice elephants in the Pāṇḍava army severed like pestles.
to create [their] faces. // 4 //
Chamberlain: Victory to the Great King!
By the command of the Great King, the entire circle of kings has been assembled.
Duryodhana has acted rightly;
you may enter the inner apartments.
Chamberlain: As the Great King commands.
[Exit.]
Duryodhana said:
"O noble ones, let Vaikarṇa and Varṣadeva be told:
'I possess a collection of eleven akṣauhiṇīs of forces; who is there [to match] this?'"
"He ought to become the commander-in-chief.
"What do you two say?
"This matter is indeed great."
Having consulted together, it should be said:
"This is appropriate;
therefore, please come, let us enter the chamber of counsel."
I salute the teacher;
may you enter the mantra-hall.
I salute the grandfather; may you enter.
"Sir, the council chamber!
Uncle, I salute you!
Sir, please enter the council chamber! Noble sirs!"
"May you two enter Vaikarṇa and Varṣadeva.
O all you Kṣatriyas, please enter as you please!"
Friend Karṇa, let us enter for a moment. (Entering) Teacher, here is this tortoise-seat;
please be seated.
Grandfather, here is this lion-throne;
please be seated. Uncle, here is this seat of skin.
"Be seated!
May the noble Vaikarṇa and Varṣadeva be seated, sirs! O all you kṣatriyas!"
"May you sit at your ease.
"Why? Why?
"Because the Great King has not yet arrived."
Oh, what a noble duty is service!
Indeed, here I am seated;
friend Karṇa, you too sit down.
Having sat down, he said: "Noble Vaikarṇa and Varṣadeva, let it be told:
I possess a collection of forces consisting of eleven akṣauhiṇīs; who ought to be the commander-in-chief of this army?"
"What did you two say?
'The honorable King of Gāndhāra will speak. Very well;
let my maternal uncle be addressed."
"What did my maternal uncle say?
'While this venerable son of Gaṅgā stands here, who else could possibly be the commander of the army?
My maternal uncle has spoken rightly."

Let it be, let it be! Let the Grandfather himself be so! We too desire this very thing, amidst the sounds of the army's shouts, the beating of drums, and the blasts of conchs, which resemble the roar of the great ocean lashed by a violent wind.
"May the hearts of the lords of men fall along with the waters of consecration poured upon the head of the son of Gaṅgā! (5) [Entering] the Chamberlain:
Victory to the Great King!
This is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, who has come as an envoy from the camp of the Pāṇḍavas.
Duryodhana:
Stop! O Bādarāyaṇa, what, what? Is Kṛṣṇa, the servant of Kaṃsa, your Puruṣottama? Is he your cowherd?
Puruṣottama!
Your Puruṣottama has had the enjoyment of fame and territory snatched away by the descendant of Bṛhadratha; alas, having taken refuge near a king!
The conduct of his servants is such that his speech is indeed full of pride:
"Begone!"
Chamberlain: May the Great King be gracious;
in my agitation, I forgot the proper etiquette.
Duryodhana fell at his feet,
crying out, "It is a calamity!"
Among humans, there is indeed such agitation.
"Arise! Arise!
[cries] the chamberlain.
I am favored;
Duryodhana,
I am now pleased.
Who is this messenger who has arrived?
Chamberlain: A messenger named Keśava has arrived.
"Duryodhana,
Keshava"— thus it should be addressed;
this indeed is the proper form of conduct.
O kings, what is appropriate for Keśava, who has come as an envoy?
"What do you say?
That Keśava is to be honored by the offering of the guest-water (arghya)?
This does not please me."
I see that his capture here is beneficial;
however, once Vāsudeva has been captured, the Pāṇḍavas would be as if they had lost their eyes.
If the Pāṇḍavas were deprived of their intelligence and resolve,
even this entire earth would become mine without a rival. // 6 //
Furthermore, whoever shall rise to meet Keśava here shall be fined by me twelve loads of gold; therefore,
let you all be vigilant.
To himself:
"What indeed could now be the means for me not to rise up? Ah, I have found it!"
A stratagem:
[Aloud] Bādarāyaṇa, let that painted cloth be brought, upon which the dragging of Draupadī’s hair and garments is depicted.
To myself:
"I shall not rise while fixing my gaze upon that."
Of Keśava. Chamberlain: As the Great King commands.
Having gone out and re-entered:
"Victory to the Great King!
Here is that painted cloth."
Duryodhana:
Spread it out before me. Chamberlain: [Does so.]
"As the Great King commands.
Duryodhana spreads it out.
"Oh, how beautiful is this painted cloth!
Here is Duḥśāsana seizing Draupadī by the hair; and here she indeed..."
Draupadī,
her eyes wide with agitation as she was seized by Duḥśāsana,
was like the crescent moon caught within the jaws of Rāhu.
It shines. // 7 //
This evil-minded Bhīma, seeing Draupadī insulted in the presence of all the kings, has his wrath inflamed and is tossing the pillar of the assembly hall.
This Yudhiṣṭhira, endowed with truth, righteousness, and compassion, yet whose mind was distracted by the gambling match,
now causes his suppressed indignation to manifest through the casting of sidelong glances.
Vṛkodara. 8.
This is Arjuna now,
his eyes clouded with rage and his lower lip quivering, regarding that circle of enemies as mere straw,
as if he were about to annihilate them.
He gradually draws the string of the Gāṇḍīva bow, summoning all the kings.
Here Yudhiṣṭhira restrains Arjuna;
these two, Nakula and Sahadeva,
have fastened their girdles, hold shields and swords in their hands, and their facial complexions have turned pale.
With their lower lips clearly bitten, free from any fear of death, those two rushed swiftly toward my brother like two young deer toward Hari, driven by his splendor. 10.
Yudhiṣṭhira here approaches and restrains the two princes.

I am base and possessed of a perverted mind; how can you two, who know right from wrong, abandon your anger today? Those who cannot endure the humiliation of being deprived of their authority over the game of dice would find their prowess called into question among those of superior character. (11)
Thus [he spoke]. This King of Gāndhāra, a gambler casting the dice, laughed with pride as if shrinking the joy of his enemies through his own fame, while seated at his ease.
The king, skilled in policy, gazes with longing at the weeping daughter of Drupada and even scratches the earth.

Having seen her, the teacher and the grandfather stood with their faces hidden behind the edge of their garments, feeling ashamed: "Oh, the richness of his complexion! Oh, the perfection of his character!"
"Aha! What perfect execution of the lines!
This painted canvas has been most clearly depicted."
"I am pleased. Who is here?
The Chamberlain: "Victory to the Great King!"
Duryodhana:
O son of Bharadvāja, let that messenger—who was amazed merely by the vehicle borne by birds—be brought here. Chamberlain: [He shall be brought.]
"As the Great King commands.
[Exit] Duryodhana.
Friend Karṇa, it is said that today Kṛṣṇa, whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa (Vāsudeva), has arrived here as a messenger of the Pāṇḍavas, like a servant;
[we] shall hear [him].
"Friend, you too, O Karṇa, lend your ears to these womanly words of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then Vāsudeva and the chamberlain enter. Vāsudeva:

Today, indeed, by the command of Dharmarāja and out of my sincere friendship for Dhanañjaya, I have performed this unseemly mission of an envoy toward Suyodhana, who is arrogant in battle and refuses to accept what is said to him. And yet—

The forest of the Kuru lineage was destroyed in battle by the fire of Bhīma’s wrath— born from the defeat of Kṛṣṇa— and by the fierce winds of Arjuna’s arrows, while he wielded the sharp mace that shattered the frontal globes of the elephants in the enemy host. 14.

This is the camp of Suyodhana. For here are the dwellings of the kings, resembling the city of the gods, spacious and constructed at will; and here are weapon-halls filled with various types of arms and implements.
The throngs of excellent horses in the stables neigh, and the elephants trumpet;
yet this vast sovereignty is on the verge of destruction due to the humiliation of its own kin. O! 15.
A speaker of evil words, a hater of virtue, deceitful, and merciless toward his own kin—
Suyodhana, indeed, upon seeing me, will not fulfill his duty at all. 16.
"O Bādarāyaṇa, what is there to enter? The Chamberlain:
"Indeed, indeed!"
Padmanābha Vāsudeva ought to enter.
Having entered, how is it that all the Kṣatriyas, upon seeing me, have become so agitated? Enough, enough!
With agitation:
"May you sirs sit at your ease.
Duryodhana.
"How, how? Upon seeing Keśava, all the Kṣatriyas are agitated! Enough, enough with this agitation!
Remember that the punishment was previously proclaimed."
"Indeed, I have been commanded:
'Vāsudeva, having approached, say: "O Suyodhana, why do you sit [there]?"'"
Duryodhana,
falling from his seat,
thought to himself: "It is perfectly clear that Keśava has indeed arrived."
Having resolved my mind with enthusiasm, I sat there composed;
yet, by the power of Keśava,
I have been moved from my seat.
"Oh, this messenger is full of guile! [Aloud] "O messenger,
please sit on this seat."
Vāsudeva said, "O Teacher, please be seated;
O kings, headed by the son of Gaṅgā, may you sit at your ease."
We too shall sit down.
Having sat down:
Oh, how beautiful this painted canvas is! Wait a moment.
The dragging of Draupadī’s hair and garment is depicted here.
Alas!
Suyodhana, out of sheer folly, looks upon this humiliation of his own kin as a display of prowess.
Who indeed in this world, devoid of shame, would personally expose his own faults in assemblies? 18.
"Āḥ! Let this painted cloth be removed!
Duryodhana said, "O Bādarāyaṇa, let the painted cloth indeed be removed!"
Chamberlain: As the Great King commands. [He removes it. Duryodhana: [Removes it.]
O messenger,
Bhīma, the son of Dharma and the son of Vāyu, my brother Arjuna, the son of the Lord of the Thirty-three, and those two self-controlled twins, the sons of the Aśvins— [all these are here].
All [his] servants have attained well-being. Vāsudeva:
This is worthy of the son of Gāndhārī; what more can be said? What more can be said?
All are well in your kingdom and in your person.
Having inquired after their external and internal welfare and their health, Yudhiṣṭhira and the other Pāṇḍavas inform him:
"Great suffering was experienced by us, and that period of time has now reached its full end."
"Let that which is our lawful inheritance also be divided," [he said]. (20)

Duryodhana asked, "How? How did he come by his inheritance? He replied, "O sir, while in the forest, my paternal uncle incurred an offense through his addiction to hunting and received a curse from a sage."
"From that moment on, being indifferent toward his wife, how could he act as a father to the children of others? O Vāsudeva,
I ask you, who are conversant with the past."
Vicitravīrya, the ruler of the realm, met his end through consumption; then,
born again from Ambikā by Vyāsa,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra indeed obtained [the kingdom].
How did Janaka [attain] sovereignty for you? 22.
Do not, do not!
O King, by thus increasing mutual hostility, the Kuru lineage will soon be nothing but a name; therefore, you ought to act accordingly.
Having set aside your anger, you [should listen] to what Yudhiṣṭhira and the others say to you out of affection.
Duryodhana said: "O messenger, you do not understand the conduct of kingship.
That which is called a kingdom is enjoyed by princes after they have conquered their enemies with the aid of their friends; it is not obtained by begging, nor indeed is it given away."
Or else, it is given to the wretched:
"If you have a desire to attain kingship, perform a daring deed without delay; or else, enter at will the hermitage favored by those of peaceful mind for the sake of tranquility. — Vāsudeva.
O Suyodhana, enough of speaking harshly to your kinsmen!
He who, having attained royal splendor through a store of merit, would deceive his friends and relatives— [what fate awaits him?]"
One's exertion would be fruitless. //25//
Duryodhana said: "O messenger,
you have no compassion for your teacher's brother-in-law, King Kaṃsa."
How could such [a state] be ours toward those who are constantly harmful? //26//
Vāsudeva said: "Enough of trying to understand that through my fault;
for you have repeatedly caused my mother to suffer the pain of separation from her son."
Having bound his own aged father, this Duryodhana has himself been slain by Death. 27.
In every way you have deceived Kaṃsa;
enough with this self-praise! This is not valor. Behold:
Then, while the Lord of Magadha was tormented by the calamity of his son-in-law’s death and overcome with rage,
[the king] fled,
overwhelmed by fear.
"Where has that valor of yours gone? [28] Vāsudeva said:
"O Suyodhana, for those who follow the path of policy, valor indeed depends upon place, time, and circumstances. Let it remain here."
Let this jest directed at us cease for now;
let your own duty be performed.
Affection should be shown toward one's brothers, and their faults should be forgotten.
Connection with kinsmen is superior for both worlds.
29. Duryodhana: How can there be kinship between gods and men? This is merely grinding what is already ground; let this discussion be cut short. 30. Vāsudeva (to himself):
Though being pacified with conciliation, he does not abandon his inherent nature;
well then, I shall agitate him with my words.
With harsh words. // 31 //
[Aloud: O Suyodhana, do you not know the strength and prowess of Arjuna?
Duryodhana: I do not know.
Vāsudeva said: "O, listen!
Paśupati, assuming the form of a Kirāta, was gratified by battle while Agni was consuming the Khāṇḍava forest."
The vast rain of arrows covered [the sky]; indeed,
at that time, the Nivātakavacas, who caused distress even to the Lord of the Gods, were brought to their destruction with ease by him alone.
In the city of Virāṭa, Bhīṣma and the others were defeated. // 32 //
Moreover, I shall tell you another thing that is evident even to you:
was it not while being carried through the sky by Citrasena during the Ghoṣayātrā that you cried out, "Phalguna!"?
He was liberated. // 33 //
What more need be said?
O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you ought to grant half the kingdom at my word;
otherwise, they will surely seize the earth bounded by the oceans.
The Pāṇḍavas! (34) How, how will Duryodhana fare? For the Pāṇḍavas shall indeed carry [the spoils] away.
Even if the Wind-god strikes in battle in his terrifying form, or if Śakra himself strikes in the guise of Pārtha;
O you who are skilled in harsh speech, I will not yield even a blade of grass from my own kingdom, which is protected by my prowess and enjoyed by my ancestors, on account of your words.
Vāsudeva:
O you who have become a stain upon the Kuru lineage, you who are greedy for infamy! We, it is said, are those who speak even to the blades of grass.
Duryodhana: [Listen!]
O cowherd, you who deserve only the name of "one who speaks of grass," having slain a woman who should not be killed, as well as a horse and a bull, you,
utterly shameless, now wish to speak even to the wrestlers!
By the virtuous ones.
Vāsudeva said: "O Suyodhana, do you not indeed insult me?
Duryodhana replied: [36]
"Is this not indeed true?
I shall go now, Vāsudeva."
Duryodhana said:
"Go, go! With your body covered by dust kicked up by the hooves of cattle, go back to the cow-pen; your time has been spent in vain."
Vāsudeva said, "So be it. We do not wish to depart without having been given a message;
therefore, let the message for Yudhiṣṭhira be heard."
The message:
"Duryodhana! Ah, you are not to be spoken to!"
With the white parasol held over me and my head sprinkled with water from the hands of the best of the twice-born, followed by a circle of kings bowing down, I converse with those like you;
I do not speak with others. (37) —Vāsudeva.
"Suyodhana indeed does not speak to me!
O rogue, devoid of affection for your kinsmen, squint-eyed crow, tawny one!
Because of you, this Kuru lineage shall soon go to its destruction. (38)
"O kings, let us depart for now;
how indeed will Keśava proceed against Duryodhana?"
O Duḥśāsana, Durmarṣaṇa, Durmukha, Durbuddhi, and Duṣṭeśvara!
Keśava has transgressed the proper conduct due to a messenger; let him be bound!
How are they powerless?
Duḥśāsana, he is not capable.
You are indeed [a fool].
That Kṛṇa, the slayer of elephants and horses, the slayer of Kaṃsa, who has never known how to subsist by living among herds of cattle—
let him be executed, his strength of arm and heroism stripped away, having brought disgrace upon himself by his own words in the presence of the kings.
Quickly! 39.
This one is powerless.
Uncle, let this Keśava be bound!
Why does he fall with his face turned away? Very well.
I myself bind him with nooses;
raising a noose, he approaches.
"How indeed does Suyodhana wish to bind Vāsudeva? Very well."
I see the power of Suyodhana; Duryodhana has assumed a universal form.
O messenger, whether you create divine illusions on all sides, or whether you strike with the irresistible weapons of the gods;
"Because you have become arrogant from felling horses, elephants, and bulls, you shall be bound by me today in the midst of the assembly of kings. (40)
Ah! Stop now!
Why has Keśava not been seen?
Here is Keśava!
"Oh, how short Keśava has become! Ah, stop right now! Why has Keśava not been seen?"
This is Keśava.
Oh, the length of Keśava’s hair! How is it not...?
Keśava has been seen;
this is Keśava. In every mantra-hall there are Keśavas. What now?
I shall do so. Very well; it has been seen.
O kings, let Keśava be bound one by one.
How is it that kings, having bound themselves with their own snares, fall?
Excellent, O Jambhaka, excellent!
Let them behold [the enemy] pierced by the nets of arrows discharged from the belly of my bow, his entire body stained with flowing blood.
The sons of Pāṇḍu, their eyes choked with tears and sighing deeply, [beheld] you brought to the camp.
Having departed, Vāsudeva thought:
"Let it be; I myself shall accomplish the task of the Pāṇḍavas."
"O Sudarśana, come here for a moment.
Then Sudarśana enters. Sudarśana:
O sir!
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, I have rushed forth with vast devotion, like a mass of clouds driven by the wind.
In what [place] indeed...
Upon whose head shall I, the lotus-eyed one, now manifest my wrath? (42)
Where indeed is the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa,
whose nature is unmanifest and inconceivable, who is intent on protecting the world,
and who, though one, possesses many forms?
The glorious one, the destroyer of the enemy's forces. // 43 //
[Looking] Ah! Here is the Blessed One, arrived at the gate of Hastināpura in the manner of an envoy.
Whence indeed could water come? Whence indeed could water come? O Blessed Ākāśagaṅgā, here is water!
Ah, it flows!
Having sipped water and approached, [he says]: "May the Blessed Nārāyaṇa be victorious! He prostrates.
O Vāsudeva,
become Sudarśana, whose prowess is unimpeded; [be] Sudarśana!
I am favored;
by good fortune, O Vāsudeva, you have arrived at the time for action.
"Sudarśana, how? How is it the time for action? May the Blessed One command; may the Blessed One command!"
Shall I overturn the ranges of Meru and Mandara, or agitate the entire ocean?
Shall I cast the whole lineage of stars down to the earth? O Lord, by your grace, nothing is impossible for me. (44)
Vāsudeva: O Sudarśana, this way, please!
O Suyodhana!

Whether you flee to the salt ocean, or into a mountain cave, or into the path of the wind frequented by the hosts of planets—O fickle one, let the Wheel of Time, set in motion today by the force attained through the power of my arms, become your end. 45.
Sudarśana: O you wretched Suyodhana, stop! Stop!
(Reflecting again)
May the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa be gracious!
For he was born upon the earth to remove the burden of the world;
O God, since this has come to pass, is it not so?
One's labor may be in vain. // 46 //
Vāsudeva, out of anger toward Sudarśana, did not observe the proper code of conduct; therefore,
you must go back to your own abode.
"Sudarśana, whatever the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa commands! How, how can he be called a cowherd?"
The Blessed One Nārāyaṇa indeed transcends the three worlds with his three strides;
you all should go to him for refuge.
I shall go. Ah!
This excellent weapon of the Blessed One, the Śārṅga bow, has been obtained;
its body is slender, soft, and graceful, it possesses the nature of a woman, and its middle is held by the hand of Hari.
The single moment of the host of enemies, with its back encrusted with gold, shines at Kṛṣṇa’s side like a beautiful streak of lightning against the flank of a fresh rain cloud. 47.
O Śārṅga, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa has calmed his anger;
you may return to your own abode. Ah, he has desisted!
I shall go now.

Ah! Here is the Kaumodakī mace obtained—variegated with jewels and gold, adorned with a wonderful garland as its upper garment, and having conceived a thirst for the destruction of the bodies of the hosts of the enemies of the gods.
Resembling the slopes of the best of mountains, irresistible and possessed of extreme power, she travels swiftly through the sky, followed by a multitude of clouds. 48.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, his anger appeased by the Kaumodakī mace—well, she has desisted;
I shall now depart. Ah! Here he is!
The Pāñcajanya conch has been obtained—
white as the full moon, the kunda flower, the water-lily, and a pearl necklace— and which received the favor of the lotus-like face of Nārāyaṇa; whose sound...
Hearing that sound, which was like the roar of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, the fetuses of the asura women fell out.
The Blessed One, whose wrath has been pacified by the Pāñcajanya conch, says:
"Go back to your own abode;
indeed, I have desisted. Oh! How wonderful!
The sword Nandaka has been obtained;
it takes the form of a woman and inspires great terror in the battle against the asuras.
He moves swiftly through the sky and shines like a great meteor. 50.
The Blessed One, whose anger has been pacified, is Nandaka.
Go back to your own abode;
indeed, he has turned back.
I shall go now. Ah!
These are the supreme weapons of the Blessed One.
This is that sword named Nandaka, which eclipses the body of the sun with its own rays. And this is she...
This very mace named Kaumodakī,
which is capable of crushing the hard chest of the enemy of the gods,
is now known as Śārṅga, its bowstring sounding like the roar of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
This is the bow-staff, this is the deep-sounding Pāñcajanya, the king of conchs, as bright as moonbeams.
O Śārṅga, Kaumodakī, Pāñcajanya, Nandaka, destroyer of the Daityas, fire to your enemies—
may your wrath be appeased.
The Blessed One, the Enemy of Mura, said:
"Go now indeed to your own abode. 52.
Ah, they have turned back!
Now I shall go.
Oh, what a violent wind this is!
The sun has passed its zenith;
the mountains have shaken;
the oceans have been stirred.
The trees fell;
the clouds wandered;
Vāsuki and the others perished.
O lords of serpents!
What indeed is this?
Ah, here comes Garuḍa, the mount of the Blessed One!
By him, for the sake of liberating his mother, the nectar—which had been obtained through the exhaustion of the gods and demons—was snatched away from his enemy Murāri;
and thus, the boon was also granted: "I shall marry you. (53)
O son dear to Kāśyapa, O Garuḍa, the Blessed One, the Lord of the gods of gods, whose anger has been pacified, says: "Go back to your own abode; indeed, I have desisted. I shall now depart."
These Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, and gods stand in the sky, their excellent crowns shaking with agitation;
when Acyuta is enraged, they lose their luster and, hearing that he has become pacified, they return to their homes, their distress allayed. (54)
"I too shall go to the lovely cave of Mount Meru.
He departed. Vāsudeva thought: "I too shall go to the camp of the Pāṇḍavas."
[Offstage: By no means, by no means must you go! Vāsudeva:
Ah, it is like the voice of the aged king!
"O King, here I am, standing.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra enters.
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, where indeed is the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa? Where indeed is the Blessed One who brings welfare to the Pāṇḍavas? Where indeed...
Where indeed is the Blessed One, who is dear to the brahmins? Where indeed is the Blessed One, the delight of Devakī?
O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, O sovereign of the thirty gods, because of the offense committed by my son, I have now fallen at your feet.
The head falls! Vāsudeva: Alas, what a tragedy! His Honor has fallen! Arise, arise!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I am graced, O Blessed One; please accept this water for honor and this water for the feet."
Vāsudeva accepts everything. What further favor may I offer you?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, what more than this could I desire? Vāsudeva replied:
May you go for the sake of seeing us again.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "As the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa commands."
[He] has departed.
[The] Bharata-vākya:
This earth, bounded by the ocean and adorned with the Himavat and Vindhya mountains as its earrings—
May that lion among kings rule over our earth, marked by the single royal parasol. 56.
All have departed;
the message of the messenger is concluded.
